Colombia Violence & Crime Data Dashboard

A free interactive panel for exploring violence and crime data in Colombia, open in the browser with no signup — and the reading guide you need before you quote a single figure from it.

The short answer

The Colombia Violence & Crime Dashboard is a free interactive panel for exploring violence and crime data in the country from your browser, with no signup or download, best read alongside an explanation of how crime statistics are actually constructed.

What the dashboard is for

Crime data is easy to find and hard to use. The numbers are published, generally consistent between institutions, and free to consult. The difficulty is not access. It is that almost every figure circulating in public debate has been detached from at least one of the things that makes it mean what people think it means.

A free interactive panel is useful for exactly one reason: it lets you move through the data yourself instead of receiving a conclusion. The moment you can change the geography, the period or the measure, you can see which claims survive and which were an artefact of how the number was presented.

How to read crime statistics in colombia without being misled

Five traps account for most of the misreporting in this subject, and all five are things a dashboard can teach you directly by letting you see the same quantity under two definitions.

None of this is a claim that anyone is lying. It is a description of how statistics get separated from their definitions in transit, which happens to honest people under deadline.

The five traps, and what to check
TrapWhat goes wrongWhat to check
DefinitionDifferent institutions count different thingsThe definition attached to the series, not just its name
Registration lagRecent years look artificially calmYear of occurrence, not year of registration
Absolute countsBigger city, bigger number, no insightRate per 100,000 inhabitants
National averageThe average hides the places that matterDepartment and municipality level
Reporting behaviourNot every crime is reported or recordedCompare homicide with lower-level crime

Difference between year of occurrence and year of registration

This is the most important single trap, and the one that catches even careful analysts. An offence has a year in which it happened and a year in which it was recorded, and those are not the same year. Records are completed, certified and published on a lag, so the most recent years are always incomplete.

The practical consequence is a pattern that reliably misleads in the same direction: the newest year looks like a decline, because the cases that have not been processed yet are not in the count. A chart that stops at the last complete year and shows the partial year in a different colour is doing the honest thing. A chart that just stops is producing an apparent improvement that is an administrative artefact.

The minimum test before you cite any figure

Ask three questions. Which definition is being used? Which year is it measured in - occurrence or registration? And what is the denominator? If any of the three cannot be answered from the source itself, the figure is not yet quotable, however confident it sounds.

Crime rate per 100000 inhabitants, and why the denominator matters

A count of homicides is mostly a count of how many people live somewhere. Comparing Bogotá to a small municipality on raw numbers tells you about population and nothing about safety. The comparable measure is a rate per 100,000 inhabitants, which normalises the two.

That normalisation introduces its own problem, because the denominator comes from a population projection that changes, and small populations produce unstable rates: a town of twenty thousand can swing several points on the rate from three or four additional cases. For municipalities, the multi-year average is almost always the more informative figure, and a single-year rate is usually noise.

Colombia’s case adds one more layer worth naming. Violence is not distributed evenly across the national territory. A handful of departments and a small set of municipalities carry a disproportionate share of the national total, and corridors that connect particular ports to particular inland cities carry more than the endpoints suggest. Any national average describes a distribution, not a country.

Bogotá, Medellín, Cali and Buenaventura read differently

Buenaventura and Cali behave as a connected corridor rather than as two independent cities, which is the point worth drawing from the panel: if a change in one is followed by a change in the other, you are looking at a route, not two local stories. Medellín has its own distinct profile and its own denominators. Bogotá is large enough that its rate is comparatively stable year to year. These are structural observations about how to read the data, not claims about current figures - check the current numbers yourself.

Colombia homicide data and official sources

The primary sources are public, and using them is not difficult. The temptation in journalism and in argument is to use a secondary summary instead, because a secondary summary is a single number while the primary source is a set of tables with caveats attached.

The three that matter most are listed below. Each has a different job, and which one to use depends on the question: administrative records describe what was formally recognised, health statistics describe what was medically observed, and survey-based work is the only route to the crimes that are never reported at all.

Homicide is measurable, other crime mostly is not

A death leaves a body, a coroner and a legal process, which is why homicide is the one violent crime with reasonably complete records. Robbery, assault and sexual violence depend on reporting, and reporting depends on trust in the institutions, on expectations about whether it will help, and on who is asking. Comparing trends in reported robbery against trends in recorded homicide as if they measured the same world is the single most common error in public debate about Colombian security.

What each official source is good for
SourceCoversGood for
DANENational statistics across sectorsPopulation denominators and official series
Instituto Nacional de Medicina LegalForensic examination of deathsCause of death in homicide cases
Policía NacionalReported and recorded crimeOffence-level counts and geographic detail
International comparisonsCross-country datasetsOnly with consistent definitions and years

Making your own charts without uploading anything

The moment you have a series you want to show someone else, you are holding data about a real place and usually about real people, and the sensible default is not to send it to a web service you do not control. PixelLibre produces the chart, the crop and the export entirely in your browser, with no account and nothing uploaded, which makes it a reasonable default for anything you intend to publish.

The practical discipline is simple: cite the series, the institution, the definition and the period every time, in the caption rather than in the discussion. A chart that carries its own caveats does more work than a paragraph defending it.

From a reading of the data to a decision about it

Knowing that a series moved does not tell you what to do, and this is where most public argument runs off the rails: a measurement is treated as a mandate. The step between them is a judgement about risk, and a judgement about risk is a judgement like any other - it depends on what you are trying to protect, how much certainty you require, and what you can afford to be wrong.

is the written treatment of acting when the result is not guaranteed by the quality of your reasoning, which is a more accurate description of this problem than any statistical method. And for the pattern of thinking this page is actually about - measure first, interpret second, commit third - the free tools on this site are the rehearsal.

Colombia Violence & Crime Dashboard: FAQ

Is the dashboard free?
Yes. It opens directly in the browser, with no registration, no download and no payment.
Do I need an account to see the data?
No. The panel is consulted directly from the browser.
Which official body publishes crime statistics in Colombia?
Several, for different purposes. DANE publishes official national statistics including population denominators, Medicina Legal covers forensic causes of death, and the Policía Nacional publishes recorded offences. The definitions differ, which is why it matters which one a figure came from.
Why does the most recent year always look like a decline?
Because offences are recorded on a lag after they occur. The newest years are incomplete, so a chart that stops at the last complete year understates them. This is the year of occurrence versus year of registration problem, and it is the most common way crime figures mislead.
Why use a rate per 100,000 instead of the raw number of cases?
Because a raw count mostly measures population. A rate normalises for size, which makes cities comparable - but for small municipalities the rate becomes unstable, and a single year is usually noise rather than a trend.
The panel does not load. What should I do?
Open the dashboard in a new tab from the link in the central block. If it still does not respond, it is likely an issue with the host rather than with your connection.
Is the interface in English?
No. The panel is in Spanish, as it was built.
